text:
maria: Noticed another gotcha in the Go generator stream sample during load testing. If the incoming HTTP request has a short deadline the SDK sometimes leaves a server job running until runtime idle timeout. Repro and notes below.

maria: Minimal repro (handler):
```go
func HandleGen(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    ctx := r.Context() // important: use request context
    req := sdk.GeneratorRequest{...}
    stream, err := client.Generator().Stream(ctx, &req)
    if err != nil { http.Error(w, "gen err", 500); return }
    defer stream.Close()
    for {
        tok, err := stream.Recv()
        if err != nil { break }
        w.Write(tok.Data)
    }
}
```

dave: ack. We saw this too. In our run ctx had 2s deadline, Cancel triggered client-side but server still kept the task for ~20s.

tess: does the runtime log show a graceful abort or a normal completion?

maria: runtime logs show stream started, then no explicit abort frame; runtime eventually garbage collected the allocation. No auth errors in this trace, but in separate tests when token refresh overlapped we saw the handshake retried and clashed with a new stream.

randall: two orthogonal issues: (A) sample app examples sometimes use context.Background() which is bad, (B) client transport closing doesn't always propagate an abort control to runtime. Suggest we: 1) update onboarding sample to show context propagation + defer Close + explicit Cancel, 2) add a Stream.Cancel() method that emits a control frame and waits N ms before closing transport, 3) make the auth refresh path check ctx.Done() and avoid re-handshake if canceled.

maria: +1 on all. Also propose exposing stream.WithCancel wrapper: if user calls stream.Cancel() we send cancel and return quickly. API example:
```go
stream, err := client.Generator().Stream(ctx, req)
defer stream.Close()
// handler wants a fast abort:
go func() {
   select{ case <-time.After(50*time.Millisecond): stream.Cancel() }
}()
```

dave: small UX nit: users keep forgetting defer stream.Close(); sample should linter-enforce pattern. Maybe add an example lint rule in the onboarding repo.

tess: about testing: we need an integration that simulates server-handshake pause and then client cancel during handshake. Then assert server goroutine count or job slots released within a short window. I can add a harness in integration/stream-cancel.

randall: runtime owners: if a cancel control frame arrives we must earliest-opinion: stop model execution, drop KV locks, and signal client-close. Also make handshake idempotent so retries on token refresh don't create duplicate in-progress jobs.

maria: filed issue: https://github.com/redwood-inference/go-sdk/issues/350 (handshake+cancel race + sample update). Added logs and heap/goroutine dump.

ci-bot: Tagged issue #350 with labels: dx, regression, needs-runtime. Triggered integration job `int-stream-cancel`.

dave: for backward compat we should make Stream.Cancel() optional; default behavior unchanged. But add a note in release notes urging passing handler context.

tess: I'll open PR with test harness + sample README change. Also adding a small unit test mocking token refresh racing with ctx cancellation.

maria: thanks — assigning SDK PR to tess, runtime follow-up to @eng-runtime. We'll verify integration job results before merging onboarding changes. :rocket:

randall: fwiw we could also document an explicit pattern for long-running inference: use a dedicated route with longer timeouts and an async response channel; avoid coupling user HTTP deadline to model compute unless user expects cancellation semantics.

maria: good call. I'll add that as a subsection in onboarding: "When to use synchronous streaming vs async job".

ci-bot: integration `int-stream-cancel` succeeded on a smaller cluster, flagged runtime owners for manual review.

maria: Ok closing thread for now, will follow up with PR links once they exist. Thanks everyone.
